=== stagedctl --help ===
Control a running Staged app from the command line.

stagedctl is built for agents running inside Staged-spawned sessions: the
app injects $STAGEDCTL_LOCK into those sessions — a per-session credential
file — and stagedctl uses it to find the app and authenticate with zero
configuration. The credential covers the session's own project and the
projects the session created (see `stagedctl project create --help`),
and is revoked when the session ends; it is the only credential a
spawned session is issued, and a session must not try to obtain wider
access (see `stagedctl connect --help`). Outside a session it tries each
running Staged instance (~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json), newest
first, until one answers, and authenticates with a connected-app grant
if `stagedctl connect` has been approved on this machine; without any
credential the app refuses commands (exit 4). Control files are read
only when they are owner-private (0600 inside a 0700 directory, no
symlinks). An empty $STAGEDCTL_LOCK is an error (exit 3), never a
fallback to the instance file.

Addressing:
  <project>   a project name or id, as printed by `stagedctl project list`
  --repo      a repo address of the form <owner>/<repo>[:<subpath>], as
              printed by `stagedctl project get <project>`
  <tag>       a tag id, <group>/<name>, or a bare tag name when only one
              tag has it, as printed by `stagedctl tag list`
  <group>     a tag group name or id, as printed by `stagedctl tag list`
  <note>      a note's hashtag reference, #note:<id> or #project-note:<id>,
              as printed by `stagedctl timeline show`; quote it, or leave
              the # off (an unquoted # starts a shell comment)

Ids print in hashtag reference form (#note:<id>, #project-note:<id>,
#review:<id>, #commit:<sha>) so they can be pasted directly into session
prompts. Every command also accepts --json for machine-readable output.

Exit codes:
  0  success
  1  command failed (stderr carries `code: message`)
  2  transport fault talking to the app
  3  no running Staged app, or the app was updated (restart Staged)
  4  not authorized: no credential (run `stagedctl connect` outside a
     session), the request was denied, the credential was revoked or
     expired, a grant file no longer matches the app's record (run
     `stagedctl disconnect` then `stagedctl connect`), or the command
     addresses something outside the credential's scope (report it; do
     not retry)

Usage: stagedctl [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>

Commands:
  project     Inspect and create projects, attach repos to them, and show one in the app
  timeline    Read project and repo timelines (commits, notes, reviews, images)
  session     Start, observe, wait for, and cancel agent sessions
  image       Attach images to a repo's timeline
  note        Move and copy notes between projects
  tag         Read and edit the tag catalog: tag groups, tags, and which projects carry them
  connect     Ask the Staged user to approve this client (outside a spawned session)
  disconnect  Forget this machine's connected-app grants and revoke them in Staged
  help        Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  -V, --version
          Print version

=== stagedctl project --help ===
Inspect and create projects, attach repos to them, and show one in the app

Usage: stagedctl project [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>

Commands:
  list      List every project in the app
  get       Show one project's repos and branches
  open      Show a project in the Staged window and bring that window to the front
  create    Create a project, optionally with its first repo
  add-repo  Attach a repo to a project, with one branch
  tags      Show one project's tags: its choice in each group, then its free tags
  tag       Tag a project: pick its tag in a group, or add free tags
  untag     Untag a project: remove the named tags, or clear its choice in a group
  help      Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help

=== stagedctl project list --help ===
List every project in the app.

Each line shows the project name, its primary repo address, where its
branches run (local or remote), and the project id. Both the name and the
id are accepted anywhere a <project> argument is expected.

Under a session's own credential the list holds the session's own
project and the projects it created with `stagedctl project create`.
Under a connected-app grant approved for one project it holds that
project.

With --tag, only the projects carrying that tag are listed. Repeating the
flag narrows further: a project must carry every tag named (AND), even
when the tags are in the same group.

Usage: stagedctl project list [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --tag <TAG>
          Only projects carrying this tag (id, <group>/<name>, or a bare name); repeat to require several

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl project get --help ===
Show one project: every attached repo with its address, and every branch
with its base branch, PR status, and worktree location.

The printed repo addresses (<owner>/<repo>[:<subpath>]) are exactly what
the --repo flag of `timeline show`, `session start`, `session list`, and
`image add` expects.

Usage: stagedctl project get [OPTIONS] <PROJECT>

Arguments:
  <PROJECT>
          Project name or id (see `stagedctl project list`)

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl project open --help ===
Show a project in the Staged app. The Staged window you were last in is
brought to the front and switched to the project: the window that holds
focus, or else the one that held it most recently and is still open.
Prints the project's name and id and the pid of the Staged instance that
showed it. A project that is already on screen is a success too.

With no <project>, the project is the one whose workspace the current
directory is in: any directory under
~/.staged/workspaces/<local|remote>/projects/<project-id>/, where Staged
keeps a project's worktrees. From any other directory the command exits 1
(`not_in_workspace`) without looking for the app; pass a <project> there.

A <project> that matches nothing (`not_found`), or several projects when
case is ignored (`ambiguous`), exits 1 before any window is touched. So
does a directory whose project the app does not list (`not_found`): the
worktree of a project that was deleted, or of one that a grant confined
to another project does not reach.

Otherwise the window is raised whether or not it could switch, so the
user sees what is in the way. When it could not, the command exits 1:
  ui_busy     a dialog is open in the window, or the diff comment being
              written could not be saved: close or finish it and run the
              command again. Also when another `project open` replaced
              this one before the window answered it.
  ui_timeout  the window did not answer in time
  not_found   the project was deleted meanwhile

Needs a connected-app grant with write access that reaches the project
(see `stagedctl connect --help`): showing a project marks it read and
records it as the last one shown, so a read-only grant is refused (exit
4, `scope_denied`). Not for Staged-spawned sessions: the app refuses a
session's credential the same way, for the session's own project too, so
an agent cannot pull the user's window away.

When Staged is not running, the command starts it, waits for it to come
up, and then asks as above; the app holds the request until its window
has loaded. A window that is still loading is not shown early: it comes
to the front once it is ready, which can be after the command has
exited. What it starts is the Staged.app this stagedctl is bundled in,
and nothing else. A line on stderr says so; stdout is unchanged. A
Staged that is running but too busy to answer is treated the same way:
opening the app only brings it forward, and the command uses it as soon
as it answers.

Staged is never started:
  - with --no-launch: the command exits 3 instead;
  - when --lock-path or $STAGEDCTL_LOCK names a control file. That
    points at one instance, and when it is gone the command exits 3, so
    a spawned session never starts an app;
  - when this machine holds no unexpired connected-app grant (exit 4,
    `authorization_required`). Start Staged and run `stagedctl connect`
    once; the consent dialog is not raised for you;
  - from a development build, whose app needs its dev server (exit 3).
    Run `just dev`;
  - beside a Staged that is running but cannot be used, such as one
    that was updated underneath this CLI (exit 3).
A <project> name is looked up only once the app is up, so a name that
matches nothing still exits 1 (`not_found`) after Staged has started. A
directory outside every project workspace never starts it.

Usage: stagedctl project open [OPTIONS] [PROJECT]

Arguments:
  [PROJECT]
          Project name or id (see `stagedctl project list`); omit it to open the project the current directory belongs to

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --no-launch
          Exit 3 instead of starting Staged when it is not running

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl project create --help ===
Create a project. Without --repo it is empty; attach repos afterwards
with `stagedctl project add-repo`. With --repo, that repo becomes the
project's primary repo and gets one branch:

  --branch   an existing remote branch, or the name of a new one. When
             the branch has an open pull request, the pull request is
             linked as with --pr.
  --pr       the pull request's branch and base. A pull request from a
             fork is found through the fork or its parent repo. Its
             description is saved as a project note titled
             "PR #<number>: <title>".
  neither    a new branch named after the project, with the user's
             branch prefix, as the New Project form does when its
             branch field is left blank.

--base is the branch a new branch starts from and the one the branch is
compared against (main and origin/main mean the same). Without it the
repo's default branch is used. A --base the repo does not have is
refused, and so is a branch name git would not accept.

The app checks the repo the way the New Project form does, before it
writes anything: the repo must exist on GitHub, a subpath must be a
directory in it, and the root of a monorepo (20 or more modules) is
refused unless --allow-monorepo-root is given. Name the subpath of the
service or package to work in where there is one. Project names are
unique: a name another project has is refused.

--location is local unless given. The location the New Project form
remembers is neither read nor changed.

  local    Staged creates a git worktree for the branch on this machine
           and then runs the repo's setup actions, in the background.
  remote   The branch runs in a Blox workspace, which Staged provisions.
           This needs the `sq` CLI and is refused without it; it never
           falls back to a local project. The workspace starts while a
           Staged window is open.

The command returns once the project exists; setup carries on in the
background, and a failure there is written to the app's log, not
reported here. `stagedctl project get` shows the branch's worktree once
it exists.

A session may create projects. Its credential covers its own project
and the projects it created, in later runs of the session too, so it
can add repos to a created project, read it and start sessions in it.
The allowance is shared along a chain of sessions: a session, the
sessions it starts and the sessions those start in turn may together
hold at most 10 created projects at a time. It makes no difference how
a session was started: with `stagedctl session start`, or by a project
session handing work to a repo session. Deleting one of those projects
in Staged frees a slot. A connected app approved for every project may
create without that limit. One approved for a single project may not
create (exit 4, `scope_denied`): reconnect without --project.

The project shows at once in the app's sidebar, where the user can
delete it. stagedctl has no delete.

Usage: stagedctl project create [OPTIONS] <NAME>

Arguments:
  <NAME>
          The project's name; must not be another project's

Options:
      --location <LOCATION>
          Where the project's branches run

          Possible values:
          - local:  Git worktrees on this machine
          - remote: A Blox workspace
          
          [default: local]

      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

      --repo <REPO>
          The project's first repo, <owner>/<repo>[:<subpath>]; default: no repo

      --branch <BRANCH>
          An existing remote branch, or the name of a new one; default: a new branch named after the project (needs --repo, not with --pr)

      --pr <NUMBER>
          A pull request number: use its branch and base (needs --repo, not with --branch or --base)

      --base <BRANCH>
          The base branch; default: the repo's default branch (needs --repo, not with --pr)

      --allow-monorepo-root
          Accept the root of a monorepo (needs --repo)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl project add-repo --help ===
Attach a repo to a project, with one branch. <PROJECT> is a name or id
among the projects this credential covers (see `stagedctl project
list`).

--repo names the repo and, for part of a monorepo, its subpath. One repo
may be attached several times under different subpaths. A repo and
subpath the project already has is refused before anything is written
(exit 1, `already_attached`), naming the branch it has there.

The branch is chosen as in `stagedctl project create`: --branch for an
existing remote branch or a new one, --pr for a pull request's branch
and base (its description is saved as a project note), neither for a
new branch named after the project. --base is the branch a new branch
starts from; without it the repo's default branch is used. A branch the
same repo already has in the project is refused, since a branch can be
checked out once per project.

The app checks the repo before it writes anything: the repo must exist
on GitHub, a subpath must be a directory in it, and the root of a
monorepo (20 or more modules) is refused unless --allow-monorepo-root is
given. The first repo a project gets becomes its primary repo.
stagedctl cannot change which repo is primary.

--reason says why the repo was added. It is shown on the repo's branch
card in the app.

What starts depends on where the project runs, and all of it is in the
background after the command returns:

  local    Staged creates a git worktree for the branch on this machine
           and then runs the repo's setup actions.
  remote   The repo is cloned into the project's Blox workspace, which
           must be running. The first repo of a remote project has no
           workspace to join: its branch provisions one, which starts
           while a Staged window is open.

A failure in that setup is written to the app's log, not reported here.

Needs write access to the project (exit 4, `scope_denied`, under a
read-only credential). A session may add repos to its own project and to
the projects it created; it cannot address any other. The repo shows at
once in the project, where the user can remove it. stagedctl has no
remove.

Usage: stagedctl project add-repo [OPTIONS] --repo <REPO> <PROJECT>

Arguments:
  <PROJECT>
          Project name or id (see `stagedctl project list`)

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --repo <REPO>
          The repo to attach, <owner>/<repo>[:<subpath>]

      --branch <BRANCH>
          An existing remote branch, or the name of a new one; default: a new branch named after the project (not with --pr)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

      --pr <NUMBER>
          A pull request number: use its branch and base (not with --branch or --base)

      --base <BRANCH>
          The base branch; default: the repo's default branch (not with --pr)

      --reason <TEXT>
          Why the repo is being added; shown on its branch card

      --allow-monorepo-root
          Accept the root of a monorepo

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl project tags --help ===
Show one project's tags.

One line per tag group, in the app's group order, with the tag the project
has in that group or (none). A last line lists the project's ungrouped
tags. The group marked as the project icon is the one whose tag draws the
project's icon in the sidebar and grid.

Usage: stagedctl project tags [OPTIONS] <PROJECT>

Arguments:
  <PROJECT>
          Project name or id (see `stagedctl project list`)

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl project tag --help ===
Tag a project. Each <tag> is applied in the order given: a grouped tag
becomes the project's choice in that group, replacing whatever it had
there (a project holds one tag per group); an ungrouped tag is added to
the project's free tags. Tags the project already carries are left as
they are. Naming two tags from the same group in one call is refused
before anything is written.

A <tag> that no tag in the catalog answers to exits 1 (`not_found`) and
writes nothing. With --create, each such bare name is instead created as
a new ungrouped tag with an automatic colour and added to the project in
the same step, which is what the tag picker's "Create tag" row does.
--create never creates a tag inside a group: use `stagedctl tag create
--group` for that, or name an existing tag.

Everything this verb does shows in the project header, where it can be
undone with the group pill's None or the chip's ×.

Each step is its own write on the app. If one fails, or the re-read after
them fails, the steps that landed are printed before the error; under
--json the result is { ok: false, applied: [...], error }, where each
applied row carries the request and the app's raw result only. Run
`stagedctl project tags` for the project's tags as they stand.

Usage: stagedctl project tag [OPTIONS] <PROJECT> <TAG>...

Arguments:
  <PROJECT>
          Project name or id (see `stagedctl project list`)

  <TAG>...
          Tag id, <group>/<name>, or a bare tag name (see `stagedctl tag list`); at most one tag per group

Options:
      --create
          Create each bare name that no tag has, as an ungrouped tag

      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl project untag --help ===
Remove tags from a project. Each named <tag> is taken off the project,
whether it is a grouped tag or a free one; a tag the project does not
carry is left alone. With --group instead, the project's choice in that
group is cleared, whatever it is (the group pill's None), and no <tag>
arguments are accepted.

Everything this verb does shows in the project header, where it can be
undone by picking the tag again.

Each step is its own write on the app. If one fails, or the re-read after
them fails, the steps that landed are printed before the error; under
--json the result is { ok: false, applied: [...], error }, where each
applied row carries the request and the app's raw result only. Run
`stagedctl project tags` for the project's tags as they stand.

Usage: stagedctl project untag [OPTIONS] <PROJECT> [TAG]...

Arguments:
  <PROJECT>
          Project name or id (see `stagedctl project list`)

  [TAG]...
          Tag id, <group>/<name>, or a bare tag name (see `stagedctl tag list`)

Options:
      --group <GROUP>
          Clear the project's choice in this group (name or id) instead of naming tags

      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl timeline --help ===
Read project and repo timelines (commits, notes, reviews, images)

Usage: stagedctl timeline [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>

Commands:
  show  Show a project's timeline, or a single repo's with --repo
  help  Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help

=== stagedctl timeline show --help ===
Show a project's timeline, or a single repo's with --repo.

Without --repo this prints the whole project: its project notes, then one
timeline per repo. With --repo it prints only that repo's timeline. Items
are ordered oldest to newest and print with hashtag references (#note:<id>,
#review:<id>, #commit:<sha>, #project-note:<id>) that can be pasted into
session prompts. An item produced by a still-running session carries a
[session <status>] suffix.

Timelines are the way to find finished work: a completed session shows up
here as its artifact (commit, note, review, or image), not in
`session list`.

Usage: stagedctl timeline show [OPTIONS] <PROJECT>

Arguments:
  <PROJECT>
          Project name or id (see `stagedctl project list`)

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --repo <REPO>
          Repo address <owner>/<repo>[:<subpath>] (see `stagedctl project get`)

      --branch <BRANCH>
          Branch name, only needed when the repo has more than one branch in this project

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl session --help ===
Start, observe, wait for, and cancel agent sessions

Usage: stagedctl session [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>

Commands:
  start   Start an agent session (spends tokens; visible in the app)
  status  Show one session's status (works for finished sessions too)
  wait    Block until a session finishes (default timeout 240s)
  cancel  Cancel a queued or running session
  list    List queued, running, and disconnected sessions
  help    Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help

=== stagedctl session start --help ===
Start an agent session. This spawns a real agent that edits the worktree
and spends tokens; the session appears immediately in the app's timeline
and can be cancelled with `stagedctl session cancel`.

With --repo, starts a session on that repo's branch; --type is required
and picks the artifact the session produces: a commit, a branch note, or
a code review. Without --repo, starts a project-level session, which
researches across the whole project, writes a project note, and may fan
work out into the project's repos; --type is not allowed there.

Prints the new session id and the artifact's hashtag reference. Follow up
with `stagedctl session wait <sessionId>` to block until it finishes.

Usage: stagedctl session start [OPTIONS] --prompt <TEXT> <PROJECT>

Arguments:
  <PROJECT>
          Project name or id (see `stagedctl project list`)

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --repo <REPO>
          Repo address <owner>/<repo>[:<subpath>]; omit to start a project-level session

      --branch <BRANCH>
          Branch name, only needed when the repo has more than one branch in this project

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

      --type <TYPE>
          What the session produces (required with --repo, invalid without)

          Possible values:
          - note:   Investigate and write a note on the branch
          - commit: Make changes and commit them
          - review: Review a commit and leave comments

      --prompt <TEXT>
          The prompt for the agent

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl session status --help ===
Show one session: status (queued, running, disconnected, completed, error,
cancelled), why it ended, its provider, prompt, and working directory.

disconnected means Staged lost its connection to a remote (Blox) session
mid-turn. It is not finished: the remote turn may still be running, and
the session returns to running when Staged reattaches it.

Session ids come from `session start`, `session list`, or the [session ...]
suffixes in `timeline show`.

Usage: stagedctl session status [OPTIONS] <SESSION_ID>

Arguments:
  <SESSION_ID>
          Session id

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl session wait --help ===
Poll the app until the session reaches a terminal state: completed, error,
or cancelled. Waiting continues through queued, running, and disconnected
(a remote session whose connection dropped; its turn may still be running).

Exit 0 when the session completes. Exits 1 with `session_error` or
`session_cancelled` when it ends any other way, and with `wait_timeout`
when --timeout elapses — in that case the session KEEPS RUNNING; waiting
never cancels anything. If the session is disconnected when --timeout
elapses, the code is `session_disconnected` instead. A status this
stagedctl doesn't recognize exits 1 with `unknown_status`.

Usage: stagedctl session wait [OPTIONS] <SESSION_ID>

Arguments:
  <SESSION_ID>
          Session id

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --timeout <SECONDS>
          Seconds to wait before giving up (the session keeps running)
          
          [default: 240]

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl session cancel --help ===
Cancel a queued or running session. The session's pending artifact stays
in the timeline marked as cancelled. Undo by starting a new session.

Usage: stagedctl session cancel [OPTIONS] <SESSION_ID>

Arguments:
  <SESSION_ID>
          Session id

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl note --help ===
Move and copy notes between projects

Usage: stagedctl note [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>

Commands:
  move  Move a note, with its session, to another project
  copy  Copy a note into a project as a new standalone note
  help  Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help

=== stagedctl note move --help ===
Move a note to another project. <NOTE> is a hashtag reference as
`stagedctl timeline show` prints it: #note:<id> for a branch note,
#project-note:<id> for a project note. Quote it, or leave the # off: an
unquoted # starts a shell comment. --to is the destination, a project
name or id (see `stagedctl project list`).

This is "Move to project" in the note's menu in the app. The note keeps
its id, so its reference still resolves, and what comes with it depends
on its kind:

  branch note    lands on the destination's branch for the repo and
                 subpath the note's branch tracks (the oldest such
                 branch, when the destination has several). Its session
                 comes with it, so the transcript stays with the note,
                 and so do the images and videos in its body. Its link
                 to the project note it was written under is dropped,
                 and moving it back does not restore that link. A title
                 another note on the landing branch has gets a number:
                 "<title> (2)".
  project note   lands in the destination project with its session and
                 media, and takes its child notes along. Each child
                 lands, with its own session, on the destination's
                 branch for its repo and subpath, still linked to the
                 project note. The output lists each child by its
                 reference, with the repo and branch it landed on.
                 If the app cannot read the children back once the
                 move is done, the output says so and --json has
                 `children: null`. They moved all the same.

Commits and code reviews are not part of a note. They stay on the branch
they were made on.

A destination that does not track a repo the move needs gets it first,
the way `stagedctl project add-repo` adds one without --branch: a new
branch named after the project, set up in the background (a worktree,
or a clone into a remote project's workspace). The output names each
repo added this way. Such a repo stays in the project when a later step
of the move fails, and the error then names it: "<repo> was added to
<project> along the way and remains tracked there."

The app refuses a move, with the note left where it was (exit 1,
`app_error`, the app's own message), when:
  - the note is already in the destination project;
  - the note is still being written, or its session or a child note's
    is queued or running. Wait for it with `stagedctl session wait`;
  - the note's branch, or a child note's, tracks no repo;
  - a project note has child notes and either project runs on a remote
    workspace, or a child note is on a remote branch or on a branch
    outside the project note's own project.

Needs write access to both projects, the one the note is in and the
destination. A read-only credential is refused (exit 4, `scope_denied`).
A credential confined to some projects, which a session's is, also
exits 4 (`scope_denied`) for:
  - a note in a project it does not reach;
  - a <NOTE> that names no note of that kind: an id that does not
    exist, or a project note's id written as #note:<id>, or the other
    way round. So exit 4 can mean a mistyped reference and not a
    missing permission; the message then says "not found". A
    credential for every project gets the app's own error for it
    (exit 1, `app_error`);
  - a note whose body embeds an image or video from a project it does
    not reach, or a project note with such a child note. The move would
    carry that media into the destination.
A destination it does not reach is not among its projects and exits 1
(`not_found`). A session may move notes between its own project and the
projects it created, in either direction, and nowhere else.

A move shows at once in both projects. The user can move the note back
in the app, and `stagedctl note move` can too. stagedctl has no delete,
and cannot remove a repo a move added.

Usage: stagedctl note move [OPTIONS] --to <PROJECT> <NOTE>

Arguments:
  <NOTE>
          The note: '#note:<id>' or '#project-note:<id>' (see `stagedctl timeline show`)

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --to <PROJECT>
          The destination project, by name or id (see `stagedctl project list`)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl note copy --help ===
Copy a note into a project. <NOTE> and --to are as in `stagedctl note
move`: a hashtag reference (#note:<id> or #project-note:<id>, quoted or
without the #) and a project name or id.

This is "Copy to project" in the note's menu in the app. The original
is left exactly as it is. The copy is a new note with its own id, which
this command prints as a hashtag reference. It holds the original's
title and body as they read now, with its own copies of the images and
videos in the body, and nothing else:

  - no session. The transcript stays with the original, and the copy is
    editable in the app like a note the user wrote;
  - no link to a parent project note and no child notes. Copying a
    project note copies that one note;
  - no suggested next steps.

A copy of a branch note lands on the destination's branch for the repo
and subpath the note's branch tracks. A destination that does not track
that repo gets it first, as in `stagedctl note move`, and the output
names it. The repo stays in the project when the copy then fails, and
the error names it. A title another note on the landing branch has gets
a number: "<title> (2)". A copy of a project note lands in the
destination project and never adds a repo.

--to may be the project the note is already in. That duplicates the
note beside the original, on the same branch for a branch note.

The app refuses a copy (exit 1, `app_error`, the app's own message)
when the note has never finished being written, or when a branch
note's branch tracks no repo. A finished note whose session was resumed
and is running again can be copied, where it could not be moved: the
copy is the note as it reads now.

Needs write access to both projects, the one the note is in and the
destination, as `stagedctl note move` does. A read-only credential is
refused (exit 4, `scope_denied`). A credential confined to some
projects, which a session's is, also exits 4 (`scope_denied`) for:
  - a note in a project it does not reach;
  - a <NOTE> that names no note of that kind: an id that does not
    exist, or the other kind's id. The message then says "not found",
    and a credential for every project gets exit 1 (`app_error`);
  - a note whose body embeds an image or video from a project it does
    not reach. The copy would duplicate that media in the destination.
    A project note's child notes are not copied, so theirs do not
    count.
A destination it does not reach exits 1 (`not_found`).

A copy shows at once in the destination, where the user can delete it.
stagedctl has no delete.

Usage: stagedctl note copy [OPTIONS] --to <PROJECT> <NOTE>

Arguments:
  <NOTE>
          The note: '#note:<id>' or '#project-note:<id>' (see `stagedctl timeline show`)

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --to <PROJECT>
          The destination project, by name or id (see `stagedctl project list`)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl tag create --help ===
Create a tag. Without --group it is an ungrouped tag (a free tag any
project may carry alongside its others); with --group it joins that group,
where a project holds one tag at a time. The new tag goes last in its
group or in the ungrouped list.

Without --color the app picks the least-used colour. --icon takes a
kebab-case Lucide icon name (circle-check, flame, …); without it the tag
draws as a dot. A name is trimmed, must be 1 to 64 characters, and must
not match another tag in the same group (or another ungrouped tag),
ignoring case.

Needs a credential that reaches every project: a session's own
credential is refused (exit 4, `scope_denied`), since the catalog is
shared by every project. To create and assign an ungrouped tag from a
session, use `stagedctl project tag <project> <name> --create`.

Shows at once in Settings ▸ Tags, where the user can rename or delete it.

Usage: stagedctl tag create [OPTIONS] <NAME>

Arguments:
  <NAME>
          The tag's name

Options:
      --group <GROUP>
          Put the tag in this group (name or id); default: ungrouped

      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --color <COLOR>
          The tag's colour; default: the least-used colour
          
          [possible values: green, red, amber, blue, purple, cyan, gray]

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

      --icon <ICON>
          A kebab-case Lucide icon name; default: none (a dot)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl tag edit --help ===
Change a tag's name, colour or icon. Only the flags given change; the
rest of the tag stays as it is. --no-icon removes the icon so the tag
draws as a dot. At least one of the flags is required.

The tag keeps its id and every project carrying it, so this is how a tag
is renamed in place. The new name must not match another tag in the same
group (or another ungrouped tag), ignoring case.

The edit reads the tag, fills the unset flags from it and sends the whole
value, so a change made elsewhere (Settings ▸ Tags, another stagedctl)
between that read and the write is overwritten; the printed row is the
tag as it stands afterwards.

Needs a credential that reaches every project (exit 4, `scope_denied`,
under a session's own credential). Shows at once in Settings ▸ Tags.

Usage: stagedctl tag edit [OPTIONS] <TAG>

Arguments:
  <TAG>
          Tag id, <group>/<name>, or a bare tag name (see `stagedctl tag list`)

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --name <NAME>
          The new name

      --color <COLOR>
          The new colour
          
          [possible values: green, red, amber, blue, purple, cyan, gray]

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

      --icon <ICON>
          The new icon, a kebab-case Lucide icon name

      --no-icon
          Remove the icon

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl tag move --help ===
Move a tag: into a group with --group, out of its group into the
ungrouped list with --ungroup, or to a new place in its own group with
--group <its group> --index <n>. --index is the zero-based position in
the destination; without it the tag goes last.

Moving a tag into a group it was not in changes what it means: a project
holds one tag per group, so every project that carries the moving tag
AND already has a tag in the destination group keeps that one and loses
the moving tag. The command counts those projects and refuses with
`conflicts` (exit 1) unless --yes is given; with no such project it goes
ahead. That is the same confirmation Settings ▸ Tags asks for. A move
within a group, or out to the ungrouped list, never drops anything.

The tag keeps its id. A tag whose name matches another in the destination,
ignoring case, is refused before anything is written; rename one first.

Needs a credential that reaches every project (exit 4, `scope_denied`,
under a session's own credential). Shows at once in Settings ▸ Tags and
in the header of every project carrying the tag.

Usage: stagedctl tag move [OPTIONS] <TAG>

Arguments:
  <TAG>
          Tag id, <group>/<name>, or a bare tag name (see `stagedctl tag list`)

Options:
      --group <GROUP>
          The destination group (name or id)

      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

      --ungroup
          Make the tag ungrouped

      --index <N>
          Zero-based position in the destination; default: last

      --yes
          Go ahead when projects would lose the tag (see above)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl tag group create --help ===
Create a tag group. It goes last in the group order. A project holds one
tag from each group, and the home page can show a board with one column
per tag of the group.

--template fills the group: `status` creates the seven project statuses
Staged shipped before tags (Idea, In progress, Polishing, Needs review,
Done, On hold, Blocked), `priority` creates P0 to P3, and `blank` (the
default) creates no tags. These are the same templates as Settings ▸ Tags'
New group menu. The name is free: a second Status group may be called
"Status 2" or anything else not already a group name, ignoring case.

When no group drives the project icon yet, the new group does, as in
Settings, so projects get an icon as soon as they pick a tag from it.

Needs a credential that reaches every project (exit 4, `scope_denied`,
under a session's own credential). Shows at once in Settings ▸ Tags,
where the user can rename or delete it.

Usage: stagedctl tag group create [OPTIONS] <NAME>

  <NAME>
          The group's name

Options:
      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --template <TEMPLATE>
          The tags to create with the group

          Possible values:
          - status:   Idea, In progress, Polishing, Needs review, Done, On hold, Blocked
          - priority: P0, P1, P2, P3
          - blank:    No tags
          
          [default: blank]

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl connect --help ===
Ask the Staged user to approve this client. Use this when stagedctl runs
outside a Staged-spawned session (no $STAGEDCTL_LOCK) — from a terminal,
a script, or an agent the user started themselves.

The request appears in the Staged window as a consent dialog naming
--client, the projects it would reach, and whether it may write; the
command waits (up to --timeout seconds) for the answer. Approval stores
a grant on this machine (~/.staged/control/grants/, owner-private) that
later invocations use without asking again; it lasts thirty days from
its last use and can be revoked at any time in the app under
Settings ▸ Connected apps, or with `stagedctl disconnect`.

Exit 4 with `authorization_denied` when the user declines. A request
left unanswered for five minutes expires in the app; the default
--timeout gives up a minute earlier so an approval never lands after
this command has stopped listening for it.

Not for Staged-spawned sessions. A spawned session is issued only its
own credential, which covers its project and the projects it created,
and must not try to obtain wider access: the app refuses `connect`
(exit 4, `scope_denied`) when the caller presents a session credential
or when its process is traceable to a running session's agent, and the
CLI refuses it locally under a per-session $STAGEDCTL_LOCK. That check
is a strong default, not a sandbox — same-user processes are not a hard
security boundary — and the rule holds either way. If a task needs
wider access, say so and let the user run this command from their own
terminal.

Usage: stagedctl connect [OPTIONS] --client <NAME>

Options:
      --client <NAME>
          The name shown to the user in the consent dialog

      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

      --project <PROJECT>
          Confine the grant to one project (name or id); default: every project

      --read-only
          Ask for read access only (no starting, cancelling or attaching)

      --timeout <SECONDS>
          Seconds to wait for the user's answer
          
          [default: 240]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

=== stagedctl disconnect --help ===
Forget the connected-app grants stored on this machine and, when a Staged
app is running, revoke them there too so their live credentials stop
working at once. With --client only the grants approved under that name
are removed. Grants a Staged app cannot be reached for are still removed
locally; revoke them in Settings ▸ Connected apps if needed.

Not for Staged-spawned sessions (exit 4, `scope_denied`, when the
caller presents a session credential or its process is traceable to a
running session): a session's credential is its own, not a
connected-app grant.

Usage: stagedctl disconnect [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --client <NAME>
          Only the grants approved under this client name

      --lock-path <PATH>
          Path to the app's control file (defaults to $STAGEDCTL_LOCK, then live ~/.staged/control/<pid>/discovery.json files, newest first)

      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of human-readable text

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
